claim: osm-3 mutants were significantly protected from tunicamycin-induced ER stress.
source: We find that mutants in the intraflagellar transport protein gene osm-3 were significantly protected from tunicamycin-induced ER stress.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: osm-3 lifespan extension is dependent on DAF-16/FOXO.
source: While osm-3 lifespan extension is dependent on the key longevity factor DAF-16/FOXO, tunicamycin resistance was not.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by demographic lifespan analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: osm-3 tunicamycin resistance is independent of DAF-16/FOXO.
source: While osm-3 lifespan extension is dependent on the key longevity factor DAF-16/FOXO, tunicamycin resistance was not.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by developmental resistance assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: osm-3 mutants are protected from bacterial pathogens in a pmk-1 p38 MAP kinase dependent manner.
source: osm-3 mutants are protected from bacterial pathogens, which is pmk-1 p38 MAP kinase dependent, while TM resistance was pmk-1 independent.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by P. aeruginosa PA14 survival assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: osm-3 tunicamycin resistance is pmk-1 independent.
source: osm-3 mutants are protected from bacterial pathogens, which is pmk-1 p38 MAP kinase dependent, while TM resistance was pmk-1 independent.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by developmental resistance assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: P-glycoprotein (PGP) xenobiotic detoxification gene expression was elevated in osm-3 mutants.
source: Expression of P-glycoprotein (PGP) xenobiotic detoxification genes was elevated in osm-3 mutants and their knockdown or inhibition with verapamil suppressed tunicamycin resistance.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by quantitative PCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Knockdown of PGPs suppressed tunicamycin resistance in osm-3 mutants.
source: Expression of P-glycoprotein (PGP) xenobiotic detoxification genes was elevated in osm-3 mutants and their knockdown or inhibition with verapamil suppressed tunicamycin resistance.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by developmental TM resistance assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Inhibition of PGPs with verapamil suppressed tunicamycin resistance in osm-3 mutants.
source: Expression of P-glycoprotein (PGP) xenobiotic detoxification genes was elevated in osm-3 mutants and their knockdown or inhibition with verapamil suppressed tunicamycin resistance.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by developmental TM resistance assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The nuclear hormone receptor nhr-8 is necessary to regulate a subset of PGPs.
source: The nuclear hormone receptor nhr-8 was necessary to regulate a subset of PGPs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by quantitative PCR data showing that upregulation of pgp-3, pgp-5, pgp-11 and pgp-13 in osm-3 mutants was suppressed in the osm-3; nhr-8 double mutant (Figure 4A).

claim: Separate pathways mediate longevity, pathogen resistance, and xenobiotic detoxification in osm-3 mutants.
source: We thus identify a cell-nonautonomous regulation of xenobiotic detoxification and show that separate pathways are engaged to mediate longevity, pathogen resistance, and xenobiotic detoxification in osm-3 mutants.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by genetic epistasis experiments showing that daf-16 is required for longevity but not TM resistance, pmk-1 is required for pathogen resistance but not TM resistance, and nhr-8 is required for TM resistance but not longevity.

claim: Many chemosensory mutants in C. elegans are long-lived.
source: Many chemosensory mutants are long-lived, and this phenotype depends on the DAF-16/FOXO transcription factor that is regulated by the insulin signaling pathway (Apfeld and Kenyon, 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Longevity of chemosensory mutants depends on the DAF-16/FOXO transcription factor regulated by the insulin signaling pathway.
source: Many chemosensory mutants are long-lived, and this phenotype depends on the DAF-16/FOXO transcription factor that is regulated by the insulin signaling pathway (Apfeld and Kenyon, 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Mutations in intraflagellar transport (IFT) proteins prevent full cilia development of amphid sensory neurons.
source: One example are mutations in intraflagellar transport (IFT) proteins that prevent full cilia development of amphid sensory neurons (Inglis et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Alterations in the IFT genes osm-3 and daf-10 disrupt the development of neuronal dendrites that project toward the tip of the nose.
source: Alterations in the IFT genes osm-3 and daf-10 disrupt the development of neuronal dendrites that project toward the tip of the nose, where they are exposed to the outer environment (Inglis et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Dye filling defective (Dyf) C. elegans are defined by an inability to take up DiI into their sensory neurons.
source: Dye filling defective (Dyf) C. elegans are defined by an inability to take up DiI into their sensory neurons (Inglis et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: daf-10(m79) has a unique resistance to pathogenic bacteria that was proposed to be downstream of sensory input.
source: One such Dyf mutant, daf-10(m79), has a unique resistance to pathogenic bacteria that was proposed to be downstream of sensory input (Gaglia et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Pairs of amphid head neurons, such as ASH and ASJ, help coordinate the innate immune response to bacterial stress after infection.
source: Furthermore, pairs of amphid head neurons, such as ASH and ASJ that often become disrupted in Dyf mutants, help coordinate the innate immune response to bacterial stress after infection (Meisel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Longevity is often associated with activation of physiological stress response pathways.
source: Longevity is often associated with activation of physiological stress response pathways and has been shown to be regulated by the insulin signaling pathway in Dyf C. elegans (Apfeld and Kenyon, 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Loss of the putative chemoreceptor Or83b significantly increases lifespan in Drosophila melanogaster.
source: In Drosophila melanogaster, loss of the putative chemoreceptor Or83b has been shown to significantly increase lifespan (Libert et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Mice with ablated olfactory sensory neurons have a unique metabolic signature that protects them from deleterious effects of a high-fat diet.
source: Moreover, mice with ablated olfactory sensory neurons have a unique metabolic signature that protects them from deleterious effects of a high-fat diet (Riera et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Unbiased screens for drug resistance have independently identified the Dyf phenotype as a common feature in drug-resistant C. elegans.
source: First, unbiased screens for drug resistance have independently identified the Dyf phenotype as a common feature in drug-resistant C. elegans (Fujii et al., 2004; Ménez et al., 2016; Collins et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Selection for resistance to the anthelmintic drug ivermectin enriches for Dyf mutants in forward genetic screens.
source: Selection for resistance to the anthelmintic drug ivermectin was shown to enrich for Dyf mutants in several forward genetic screens (Ménez et al., 2016; Page, 2018; Dent et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: P-glycoproteins (PGPs) are the drivers behind ivermectin resistance in Dyf mutants.
source: Follow-up work identified P-glycoproteins (PGPs), a class of ATP binding cassette (ABC) transporters, as the drivers behind ivermectin resistance in Dyf mutants (Ardelli and Prichard, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Some chemosensory mutations, such as in daf-10, lead to resistance to pathogenic bacteria.
source: Second, some chemosensory mutations, such as in daf-10, lead to resistance to pathogenic bacteria (Gaglia et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: osm-3 is a long-lived Dyf mutant that was previously identified in a forward genetic screen for resistance to tunicamycin.
source: Here, we characterize a long-lived Dyf mutant, osm-3, that was previously identified in a forward genetic screen for resistance to the potent ER stressor tunicamycin (TM).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by reference to previous work.

claim: The hexosamine biosynthetic pathway plays a role in TM resistance and longevity.
source: From this screen, we reported the role of the hexosamine biosynthetic pathway in TM resistance and longevity (Denzel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The largest cohort of classifiable mutants from a TM resistance screen presented the Dyf phenotype.
source: The largest cohort of classifiable mutants presented the Dyf phenotype (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by reference to Figure 1A showing DiI staining.

claim: osm-3(dh441)IV has a C to T mutation at position 3796925 of exon 8.
source: osm-3(dh441)IV has a C to T mutation at position 3796925 of exon 8.
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1B caption and shown in the figure.

claim: osm-3(dh441)IV carries a premature stop in the eighth exon.
source: The mutant allele we selected for our investigation, osm-3(dh441)IV (this allele will be referred to hereafter as osm-3), carries a premature stop in the eighth exon, which prevents normal cilia development causing the Dyf phenotype (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 1B showing the mutation location.

claim: osm-3 mutants fully develop at tunicamycin concentrations at least up to 10 µg/mL.
source: While WT worms fail to develop on TM at concentrations above 4 µg/mL, osm-3 mutants fully develop at concentrations at least up to 10 µg/mL TM (Figure 1C; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by developmental TM resistance assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: WT worms fail to develop on TM at concentrations above 4 µg/mL.
source: While WT worms fail to develop on TM at concentrations above 4 µg/mL, osm-3 mutants fully develop at concentrations at least up to 10 µg/mL TM (Figure 1C; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by developmental TM resistance assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: osm-3 mutants have extended lifespan.
source: Demographic lifespan analysis of osm-3 indeed confirmed extended lifespan in our point mutant (Figure 1D and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by demographic lifespan analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: All long-lived Dyf mutants tested were significantly TM resistant at 10 µg/mL TM.
source: To our surprise, all long-lived Dyf mutants that we tested proved to be significantly TM resistant at the WT lethal dose of 10 µg/mL TM (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1—source data 1–7).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by developmental TM resistance assay data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Long-lived chemosensory odr-1(n1936)X, odr-3(n2150)V, and tax-4(p678)III mutants that do not display a Dyf phenotype were only slightly TM resistant.
source: In contrast, the long-lived chemosensory odr-1(n1936)X, odr-3(n2150)V, and tax-4(p678)III mutants that do not display a Dyf phenotype were only slightly TM resistant (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1H–J, Figure 1—figure supplement 1—source data 8–10).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by developmental TM resistance assay data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Among chemosensory defective mutants, lifespan extension is uncoupled from TM resistance.
source: Our data thus suggest that, among the larger class of chemosensory defective mutants, lifespan extension is uncoupled from TM resistance.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and inferred from the observation that some long-lived chemosensory mutants without the Dyf phenotype are not TM resistant.

claim: TM treatment activates the ER unfolded protein response (UPRER).
source: TM treatment activates the ER unfolded protein response (UPRER); we thus characterized the overall transcriptional response of osm-3 mutants upon TM treatment.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and is established knowledge about TM's mechanism of action.

claim: Gene ontology (GO) terms related to ER stress and ER protein folding showed significant upregulation in WT animals after TM treatment, but not in osm-3 mutants.
source: Notably, the gene ontology (GO) terms related to ER stress and ER protein folding showed significant upregulation in WT animals, but not in osm-3 mutants (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by transcriptomic analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: RT-qPCR analysis confirmed that there was no UPRER induction in TM-treated osm-3 mutants compared to WT.
source: RT-qPCR analysis of UPR target genes further confirmed that there was no UPRER induction in TM-treated osm-3 mutants compared to the WT (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: A hallmark of UPRER activation in C. elegans is the upregulation of the molecular chaperone HSP-4/BiP.
source: A hallmark of UPRER activation in C. elegans is the upregulation of the molecular chaperone HSP-4/BiP (Shen et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Upon TM treatment of osm-3 mutants carrying an hsp-4::GFP reporter construct, there was no significant increase in the GFP signal compared to the untreated control.
source: Upon TM treatment of osm-3 mutants carrying an hsp-4::GFP reporter construct, there was no significant increase in the GFP signal compared to the untreated control, while in the WT, the GFP levels were significantly increased (Figure 2B,C, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Biosorter analysis and fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: In WT worms, TM treatment significantly increased hsp-4::GFP levels.
source: Upon TM treatment of osm-3 mutants carrying an hsp-4::GFP reporter construct, there was no significant increase in the GFP signal compared to the untreated control, while in the WT, the GFP levels were significantly increased (Figure 2B,C, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Biosorter analysis and fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: The ER membrane protein SEL-1/HRD3 is a cofactor of the HRD1 ubiquitin ligase complex involved in ER-associated degradation (ERAD).
source: The ER membrane protein SEL-1/HRD3 is a cofactor of the HRD1 ubiquitin ligase complex involved in ER-associated degradation (ERAD) (Hampton et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Using sel-1 RNAi to inhibit ERAD resulted in robust activation of the hsp-4::GFP reporter in osm-3 mutants.
source: Using sel-1 RNAi to inhibit ERAD, we observed a robust activation of the hsp-4::GFP reporter, suggesting a functional UPRER response upon ER stress in osm-3 mutants (Figure 2D,E, Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Biosorter analysis and fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 2D,E.

claim: osm-3 mutants have a functional UPRER response upon ER stress.
source: Using sel-1 RNAi to inhibit ERAD, we observed a robust activation of the hsp-4::GFP reporter, suggesting a functional UPRER response upon ER stress in osm-3 mutants (Figure 2D,E, Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and inferred from the observation that sel-1 RNAi induces hsp-4::GFP in osm-3 mutants.

claim: DTT treatment induced normal levels of hsp-4::GFP induction and xbp-1 splicing in osm-3 mutants.
source: We further used DTT treatment to induce ER stress and found normal levels of hsp-4::GFP induction and xbp-1 splicing (Figure 2F, Figure 2—source data 3) in osm-3 mutants.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by quantitative PCR data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The reduced response to TM observed in osm-3 mutants is not due to a defect in UPR signaling.
source: Together, these observations rule out that the reduced response to TM observed in osm-3 mutants was due to a defect in UPR signaling.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and inferred from the observation that osm-3 mutants can mount a UPR response to sel-1 RNAi and DTT treatment.

claim: The lifespan extension observed in chemosensory-defective C. elegans is at least partially insulin signaling dependent.
source: The lifespan extension observed in chemosensory-defective C. elegans as well as in Drosophila has been shown to be at least partially insulin signaling dependent (Apfeld and Kenyon, 1999; Libert et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The osm-3 lifespan extension is fully daf-16 dependent.
source: Indeed, the osm-3 lifespan extension was fully daf-16 dependent, as the lifespan of the osm-3; daf-16 double mutants was identical to the daf-16 lifespan (Figure 3A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by demographic lifespan analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The osm-3; daf-16 double mutant remained resistant to TM while daf-16 single mutants do not develop at 10 µg/mL TM.
source: In stark difference to osm-3 survival, the osm-3; daf-16 double mutant remained resistant to TM while daf-16 single mutants do not develop at 10 µg/mL TM (Figure 3B, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by developmental resistance assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Knockdown of daf-16 by RNAi did not elevate the hsp-4::GFP response of osm-3 mutants after TM treatment.
source: Interestingly, knockdown of daf-16 by RNAi did not elevate the hsp-4::GFP response of osm-3 mutants after TM treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Biosorter analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: daf-2 mutants failed to develop on 10 µg/mL TM, while osm-3 mutants were fully developed.
source: Given the links between the insulin signaling pathway and ER stress signaling (Henis-Korenblit et al., 2010; Kyriakakis et al., 2017; Matai et al., 2019; Labbadia and Morimoto, 2014), we were surprised to find that daf-2 mutants failed to develop on 10 µg/mL TM, while osm-3 mutants were fully developed (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by developmental resistance assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The osm-3 lifespan extension and TM drug resistance are uncoupled and act via independent pathways.
source: Together, this evidence suggests that the osm-3 lifespan extension and TM drug resistance are uncoupled and act via independent pathways.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and inferred from the observation that daf-16 is required for longevity but not TM resistance.

claim: The PMK-1 p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway has been implicated in the innate immune response of C. elegans during PA14 infection.
source: The PMK-1 p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway as well as UPRER targets have been implicated in the innate immune response of C. elegans during PA14 infection (Richardson et al., 2010; Haskins et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: osm-3 mutants were resistant to PA14.
source: Indeed, osm-3 mutants were resistant to PA14, and this increased pathogen resistance was lost upon pmk-1 knockdown (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by P. aeruginosa PA14 survival assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The increased pathogen resistance of osm-3 mutants was lost upon pmk-1 knockdown.
source: Indeed, osm-3 mutants were resistant to PA14, and this increased pathogen resistance was lost upon pmk-1 knockdown (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by P. aeruginosa PA14 survival assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The osm-3; pmk-1 double mutant was fully resistant to TM, while the pmk-1 single mutant was sensitive.
source: The osm-3; pmk-1 double mutant was fully resistant to TM, while the pmk-1 single mutant was sensitive (Figure 3D, Figure 3—source data 2), demonstrating that TM resistance and pmk-1 mediated pathogen resistance are uncoupled in osm-3 mutants.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by developmental resistance assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: TM resistance and pmk-1 mediated pathogen resistance are uncoupled in osm-3 mutants.
source: The osm-3; pmk-1 double mutant was fully resistant to TM, while the pmk-1 single mutant was sensitive (Figure 3D, Figure 3—source data 2), demonstrating that TM resistance and pmk-1 mediated pathogen resistance are uncoupled in osm-3 mutants.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and inferred from the observation that pmk-1 mutation does not suppress osm-3 TM resistance.

claim: Insulin signaling and the MAPK pathway are not required for TM resistance in osm-3 mutants.
source: Taken together, insulin signaling and the MAPK pathway, two major stress response pathways in C. elegans that have links to ER protein quality control, are not required for TM resistance in osm-3 mutants.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and inferred from the genetic epistasis experiments showing that daf-16 and pmk-1 mutations do not suppress osm-3 TM resistance.

claim: PGPs are a conserved family of ATP binding cassette (ABC) transporters that locate to the cell membrane.
source: PGPs are a conserved family of ATP binding cassette (ABC) transporters that locate to the cell membrane (Sangster, 1994) and they are involved in toxin clearance.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: C. elegans have 15 pgp genes.
source: C. elegans have 15 pgp genes.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and is established knowledge about C. elegans.

claim: There is significant upregulation of pgp-3, pgp-5, pgp-11, and pgp-13 in osm-3 mutants.
source: Using quantitative PCR, we found a significant upregulation of pgp-3, pgp-5, pgp-11, and pgp-13 in osm-3 mutants (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by quantitative PCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The nuclear hormone receptor NHR-8 has been linked to xenobiotic detoxification and pgp regulation in C. elegans.
source: The nuclear hormone receptor NHR-8 has been linked to xenobiotic detoxification and pgp regulation in C. elegans (Ménez et al., 2019; Lindblom et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The upregulation of pgp-3, pgp-5, pgp-11 and pgp-13 in osm-3 mutants was suppressed in the osm-3; nhr-8 double mutant.
source: Indeed, we found that the upregulation of pgp-3, pgp-5, pgp-11 and pgp-13, in osm-3 mutants, was suppressed in the osm-3; nhr-8 double mutant (Figure 4A, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by quantitative PCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Knockdown of pgp-5, pgp-11, and pgp-12 partially reduced the TM resistance of the osm-3 mutants.
source: Interestingly, knockdown of pgp-5, pgp-11, and pgp-12 partially reduced the TM resistance of the osm-3 mutants (Figure 4B, Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by developmental TM resistance assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Verapamil has been used to specifically inhibit PGP activity, re-sensitizing worms to the anthelmintic compound ivermectin.
source: Verapamil has been used to specifically inhibit PGP activity, re-sensitizing worms to the anthelmintic compound ivermectin (Ménez et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: 1 nM verapamil significantly suppressed development of osm-3 C. elegans in the presence of TM.
source: Indeed, 1 nM verapamil significantly suppressed development of osm-3 C. elegans in the presence of TM, showing no effect on controls without TM (Figure 4C, Figure 4—source data 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by developmental TM resistance assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Verapamil showed no effect on osm-3 development on controls without TM.
source: Indeed, 1 nM verapamil significantly suppressed development of osm-3 C. elegans in the presence of TM, showing no effect on controls without TM (Figure 4C, Figure 4—source data 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by developmental TM resistance assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Xenobiotic detoxification is achieved by multiple PGPs.
source: The partial effects of pgp knockdown (Figure 4B) and verapamil treatment (Figure 4C) suggest that xenobiotic detoxification is achieved by multiple PGPs, which are likely to be transcriptionally orchestrated by nhr-8.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and inferred from the partial effects of individual PGP knockdowns and verapamil treatment.

claim: Multiple PGPs are likely to be transcriptionally orchestrated by nhr-8.
source: The partial effects of pgp knockdown (Figure 4B) and verapamil treatment (Figure 4C) suggest that xenobiotic detoxification is achieved by multiple PGPs, which are likely to be transcriptionally orchestrated by nhr-8.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and inferred from the observation that nhr-8 regulates multiple PGPs.

claim: The resistance of osm-3 mutants to TM was largely suppressed in the osm-3; nhr-8(hd117)IV double mutant.
source: Strikingly, the developmental TM assay revealed that the resistance of osm-3 mutants was largely suppressed in the osm-3; nhr-8(hd117)IV double mutant (Figure 4D. Figure 4—source data 4), suggesting that NHR-8 is necessary for osm-3 TM resistance.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by developmental TM resistance assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: NHR-8 is necessary for osm-3 TM resistance.
source: Strikingly, the developmental TM assay revealed that the resistance of osm-3 mutants was largely suppressed in the osm-3; nhr-8(hd117)IV double mutant (Figure 4D. Figure 4—source data 4), suggesting that NHR-8 is necessary for osm-3 TM resistance.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and inferred from the observation that nhr-8 mutation suppresses osm-3 TM resistance.

claim: osm-3 mutants fully developed to adults in the presence of 6 µg/mL ivermectin that is lethal to WT animals.
source: As suggested by a role of PGPs in ivermectin resistance, we found that osm-3 mutants fully developed to adults in the presence of 6 µg/mL ivermectin that is lethal to WT animals (Figure 4E, Figure 4—source data 5).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by developmental ivermectin resistance assay data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Ivermectin resistance of osm-3 mutants was suppressed by loss of NHR-8.
source: Ivermectin resistance of osm-3 mutants was suppressed by loss of NHR-8.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by developmental ivermectin resistance assay data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Dyf C. elegans mutants have been independently identified in drug resistance screens.
source: Dyf C. elegans mutants have been independently identified in drug resistance screens (Fujii et al., 2004; Ménez et al., 2016; Dent et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: osm-3 mutants were resistant to 200 nM paraquat, as they fully develop at a concentration that is toxic to WT C. elegans.
source: Consistent with these findings, we observed that osm-3 mutants were resistant to 200 nM paraquat, as they fully develop at a concentration that is toxic to WT C. elegans (Figure 4F, Figure 4—source data 6).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by developmental paraquat resistance assay data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: NHR-8 was required for the paraquat resistance of the osm-3 mutants.
source: Consistent with a role in xenobiotic detoxification, NHR-8 was required for the paraquat resistance of the osm-3 mutants (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by developmental paraquat resistance assay data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Several PGPs have been shown to be expressed in non-neuronal tissue.
source: Several PGPs have been shown to be expressed in non-neuronal tissue (Lincke et al., 1993; Sheps et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: nhr-8 has been shown to be expressed in the intestine of C. elegans.
source: Moreover, we found that PGP expression is regulated by nhr-8, which has also been shown to be expressed in the intestine of C. elegans (Magner et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Neuronal signaling controls drug resistance through nuclear hormone signaling.
source: Combining this previous information with our finding that Dyf mutants are resistant to several uniquely toxic drugs, we conclude that neuronal signaling controls drug resistance through nuclear hormone signaling.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and inferred from the observation that Dyf mutants (with neuronal defects) have increased PGP expression regulated by nhr-8.

claim: The NHR-8 ligand is likely a sterol molecule derived from cholesterol metabolism.
source: The NHR-8 ligand remains unknown, but is likely a sterol molecule derived from cholesterol metabolism (Magner et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Omitting cholesterol from the culture plates for one generation leads to TM hypersensitivity in both WT and osm-3 animals.
source: We thus tested the role of cholesterol in TM resistance and found that omitting cholesterol from the culture plates for one generation leads to TM hypersensitivity in both WT and osm-3 animals (Figure 5A, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by developmental dose-response TM resistance assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: High cholesterol significantly reduced TM-induced ER stress.
source: To specifically assess a role of cholesterol-derived signals in TM resistance, we used the hsp-4::GFP reporter and found that high cholesterol significantly reduced TM-induced ER stress (Figure 5B, Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Biosorter analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: WT TM resistance is cholesterol dependent.
source: Developmental cholesterol dose–response assays in the presence of TM confirmed that WT TM resistance is cholesterol dependent.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by cholesterol dose-response developmental assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In nhr-8 and osm-3; nhr-8 double mutants, cholesterol treatment failed to protect from TM toxicity.
source: In nhr-8 and osm-3; nhr-8 double mutants, however, cholesterol treatment failed to protect from TM toxicity (Figure 5C, Figure 5—source data 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by cholesterol dose-response developmental assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: NHR-8 plays a key role in mediating TM resistance downstream of sterol signals.
source: This demonstrates a key role of NHR-8 in mediating TM resistance downstream of sterol signals.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and inferred from the observation that cholesterol-mediated TM protection requires nhr-8.

claim: Verapamil did not shorten osm-3 lifespan.
